subject: physics

items.q: How much of a sample remains after two half-lives?
items.correct: One quarter — each half-life halves what's left (½ then ½ again).
items.misconception: None — after two half-lives it has completely decayed.
items.random_wrong: It doubles, because the decay reverses.
items.why: Each half-life halves the remaining undecayed nuclei: 1 → ½ → ¼. The amount falls in halving steps and never instantly reaches zero.

items.q: Can heating a radioactive source change its half-life?
items.correct: No — half-life is fixed for an isotope and is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemistry.
items.misconception: Yes, heating it makes it decay faster and shortens the half-life.
items.random_wrong: Half-life depends on how much of the sample you have.
items.why: Radioactive decay is a random nuclear process, independent of physical conditions or how much material is present.

items.q: What is a beta-minus particle and where does it come from?
items.correct: A fast-moving electron created in the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton.
items.misconception: An electron knocked out of the atom's outer shells.
items.why: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton plus an electron; that electron is emitted from the nucleus, not from the electron cloud.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Physics (4PH1) specification; Radioactivity & Particles
